item.title: Venus of Urbino
item.lesson: Botticelli's Venus was a goddess arriving from myth; Titian's reclines on rumpled sheets in a recognizable Venetian palazzo and looks you calmly in the eye. Painted for Guidobaldo II della Rovere, the future Duke of Urbino, she was called a Venus mostly to make her respectable — behind her, maids rummage in a wedding chest and a small dog sleeps at her feet, an old emblem of fidelity, so the picture may have marked a marriage. What made it revolutionary was Venetian color: where Florentines built pictures on drawing, Titian built them from flesh-warm paint itself, layer over layer, until skin seemed lit from within. Three centuries later Édouard Manet borrowed this exact pose for his Olympia and scandalized Paris — proof that Titian's frank gaze had lost none of its charge.
item.lookFor: Compare the two halves of the background: the dark green curtain drops like a stage flat exactly at her hip, cleanly splitting the canvas and steering your eye along the length of her body.
